title: Education is no barrier to knowing God
source_text: Ψεῦδος δὲ καὶ τὸ μόνους ἠλιθίους καὶ ἀγεννεῖς καὶ ἀναισθήτους καὶ ἀνδράποδα καὶ γύναια καὶ παιδάρια πείθειν ἐθέλειν τοὺς διδάσκοντας τὸν θεῖον λόγον. καὶ τούτους μὲν γὰρ καλεῖ ὁ λόγος, ἵνα αὐτοὺς βελτιώσῃ· καλεῖ δὲ καὶ τοὺς πολλῷ τούτων διαφέροντας· ἐπεὶ „σωτήρ ἐστιν πάντων ἀνθρώπων“ ὁ Χριστὸς καὶ „μάλιστα πιστῶν.“ εἴτε συνετῶν εἴτε ἁπλουστέρων, καὶ „ἱλασμός ἐστι“ „πρὸς τὸν πατέρα“ „περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, οὐ μόνον δὲ περὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου.“ περισσὸν οὖν τὸ θέλειν μετὰ ταῦτ᾿ ἀπολογήσασθαι ἡμᾶς πρὸς τὰς Κέλσου λέξεις οὕτως ἐχούσας· τί γάρ ἐστιν ἄλλως κακὸν τὸ πεπαιδεῦσθαι καὶ λόγων τῶν ἀρίστων ἐπιμεμελῆσθαι καὶ φρόνιμον εἶναί τε καὶ δοκεῖν; τί δὲ κωλύει τοῦτο πρὸς τὸ γνῶναι θεόν; τί δ᾿ οὐχὶ προὔργου μᾶλλον καὶ δι᾿ οὗ μᾶλλόν τις ἂν ἐφικέσθαι δύναιτο ἀληθείας; τὸ μὲν οὖν ἀληθῶς πεπαιδεῦσθαι οὐ κακόν· ὁδὸς γὰρ ἐπ᾿ ἀρετήν ἐστιν ἡ παίδευσις· τὸ μέντοι γε ἐν πεπαιδευμένοις ἀριθμεῖν τοὺς ἐσφαλμένα δόγματα ἔχοντας οὐδ᾿ οἱ Ἑλλήνων σοφοὶ φήσουσι. πάλιν τ᾿ αὖ τίς οὐκ ἂν ὁμολογήσαι ὅτι λόγων τῶν ἀρίστων ἐπιμεμελῆσθαι ἀγαθόν ἐστιν; ἀλλὰ τίνας ἐροῦμεν τοὺς ἀρίστους λόγους ἢ τοὺς ἀληθεῖς καὶ ἐπ᾿ ἀρετὴν παρακαλοῦντας; ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ φρόνιμον εἶναι καλόν ἐστιν, οὐκέτι δὲ τὸ δοκεῖν, ὅπερ εἶπεν ὁ Κέλσος. καὶ οὐ κωλύει γε πρὸς τὸ γνῶναι θεὸν ἀλλὰ καὶ συνεργεῖ τὸ πεπαιδεῦσθαι καὶ λόγων ἀρίστων ἐπιμεμελῆσθαι καὶ φρόνιμον εἶναι. καὶ ἡμῖν μᾶλλον πρέπει τοῦτο λέγειν ἢ Κέλσῳ, καὶ μάλιστ᾿ ἐὰν Ἐπικούρειος ὢν ἐλέγχηται.
pass_a_gloss: And false (ψεῦδος) also [is] that those teaching the divine word (θεῖον λόγον) wish (ἐθέλειν) to persuade (πείθειν) only the silly (ἠλιθίους) and ignoble (ἀγεννεῖς) and senseless (ἀναισθήτους) and slaves (ἀνδράποδα) and little women (γύναια) and little children (παιδάρια). For these indeed the word calls (καλεῖ), so that it may improve (βελτιώσῃ) them; but it calls also those much differing from (διαφέροντας, surpassing) these; since Christ is 'savior (σωτήρ) of all men' and 'especially of believers (πιστῶν)', whether intelligent (συνετῶν) or simpler (ἁπλουστέρων), and 'is propitiation (ἱλασμός)' 'toward the Father (πρὸς τὸν πατέρα)' 'concerning our sins (ἁμαρτιῶν), and not only concerning ours but also concerning the whole world (κόσμου)'. Superfluous (περισσόν) then [is] wishing after these things that we defend ourselves (ἀπολογήσασθαι) against Celsus's words (λέξεις) holding thus: For what otherwise (ἄλλως) is evil (κακόν) in being educated (πεπαιδεῦσθαι) and in having cared for (ἐπιμεμελῆσθαι) the best discourses (λόγων τῶν ἀρίστων) and being sensible (φρόνιμον) and seeming (δοκεῖν) so? And what does this hinder (κωλύει) toward knowing God? And what is it not rather an advantage (προὔργου), and through which one might rather be able to attain (ἐφικέσθαι) truth (ἀληθείας)? To be truly educated then is not evil; for education (παίδευσις) is a road (ὁδός) to virtue (ἀρετήν); however to number (ἀριθμεῖν) among the educated those holding erroneous doctrines (ἐσφαλμένα δόγματα) not even the wise of the Greeks will say. And again who would not agree that to have cared for the best discourses is good? But whom shall we call the best discourses, except the true ones and those summoning (παρακαλοῦντας) to virtue? But also to be sensible is fine (καλόν), but no longer the seeming (δοκεῖν), which Celsus said. And it does not hinder toward knowing God but even works with (συνεργεῖ) [it], to be educated and to have cared for the best discourses and to be sensible. And to us it is more fitting (πρέπει) to say this than to Celsus, and especially if he is convicted (ἐλέγχηται) of being an Epicurean (Ἐπικούρειος).
pass_b_english: It is false, too, that those who teach the divine word wish to persuade only “the silly, the low-born, the dull, slaves, women and little children.” The word does call these, to make them better; but it also calls those who are far above them, since Christ is “the Saviour of all men, and especially of believers” (1 Timothy 4:10), whether intelligent or simpler, and he is “the propitiation” “with the Father” “for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world” (1 John 2:1–2).

After this, then, it is needless for us to want to defend ourselves against Celsus’s words, which run thus: “For what evil is there, in any case, in being educated, in having devoted oneself to the best teachings, and in being sensible and seeming so? What hindrance is this to knowing God? Why is it not rather a help, and a means by which one might better reach the truth?”

To be truly educated, then, is no evil, for education is a road to virtue. Yet not even the wise men of the Greeks will say that those who hold mistaken doctrines should be counted among the educated. Again, who would not agree that it is good to have devoted oneself to the best teachings? But which shall we call the best teachings, if not those that are true and summon us to virtue? Being sensible is also a fine thing, but not merely seeming so, which is what Celsus said. Being educated, having devoted oneself to the best teachings, and being sensible do not hinder the knowledge of God; they even help toward it. And it is more fitting for us to say this than for Celsus, especially if he is shown to be an Epicurean.

choices.choice: The list in the first sentence repeats Celsus's own words from 3.44 (Origen turns them into an infinitive clause), so the list is set in quotation marks. ἠλιθίους is rendered 'the silly' (not 'the simple') so that it stays distinct from Origen's own approving word ἁπλουστέρων ('simpler') a few lines later. γύναια and παιδάρια are contemptuous diminutives in Celsus ('mere women', 'little children'). 1 Timothy 4:10 calls God 'Saviour of all men, especially of believers'; Origen applies the phrase to Christ, and the English follows Origen. 'With the Father' comes from 1 John 2:1 ('we have an advocate with the Father'), joined by Origen to 'propitiation' from 1 John 2:2; one citation covers the joined phrases. λόγων τῶν ἀρίστων is rendered 'the best teachings' so that Origen's follow-up ('those that are true and summon us to virtue') reads naturally; it could also be 'the best studies' or 'the finest literature'. ἄλλως in Celsus's question is rendered 'in any case'. 'Seeming so' keeps Celsus's δοκεῖν, which Origen rejects as mere appearance. The charge that Celsus is an Epicurean is Origen's recurring suspicion in this work.
ἠλιθίους: 'the simple' -> 'the silly', to keep Celsus's insult distinct from Origen's positive ἁπλουστέρων ('simpler').
1 John citations merged into one '(1 John 2:1–2)' after the joined phrases; the old first citation sat on 'with the Father' alone.
Celsus's 'what evil is there otherwise' (calque of ἄλλως) -> 'what evil is there, in any case'.
